Histological examination of ovarian tissue revealed a mean gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 6% [GSI = 6%] for females sampled from the lake's littoral zone at a stable water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This value, which describes the proportion of body mass devoted to ovarian tissue, is modest relative to some other freshwater blenniids and likely reflects an iteroparous strategy in which females partition reproductive effort across multiple spawning bouts within a single season rather than investing heavily in a single event. Additional morphometric data gathered from the same population indicate that the ultimate total length attained by adults reaches 7.3 cm [Li = 7.3 cm], placing this species among the smaller members of its genus. This asymptotic body size appears to be constrained by both the limited dimensions of its lacustrine habitat and the energetic demands of a relatively cool thermal regime, to which the local population has become adapted over evolutionary time.

The onset of reproductive capability in this species occurs when individuals reach a total length of 3 cm [Lp = 3 cm], a size threshold that corresponds to the completion of gonadal differentiation and the first detectable signs of vitellogenic activity in females. Puberty at this modest body length permits relatively early entry into the breeding population, a demographic trait that may offset the presumably high mortality experienced during the vulnerable larval and early juvenile stages. The size at which this transition occurs was verified through examination of gonadal histology across a size-grade series of freshly preserved specimens, and the estimate aligns well with the body-length trajectory documented for captive-reared cohorts. From an ecological standpoint, achieving reproductive maturity at 3 cm [Lp = 3 cm] allows individuals to begin contributing to recruitment before they have reached their ultimate dimensions, thereby increasing the likelihood that at least some offspring will be produced before the adult suffers predation or other sources of mortality common in shallow freshwater environments.

Neonates of Salariopsis economidisi emerge at an extraordinarily low wet weight of 0.0002 grams [Wwb = 0.0002 grams], a value derived from volumetric calculations based on the dimensions of the fertilised ovum, which measures 1.1 mm in length and 0.6 mm in width. This minuscule birth mass places the newly hatched prolarva squarely within the size range typical of teleosts that produce pelagic eggs, reflecting a life-history strategy in which maternal investment per offspring is low and fecundity is correspondingly high. The yolk-sac larva, possessing only this modest endogenous nutrient endowment, must quickly develop the capacity for exogenous feeding to sustain further growth. The developmental interval from fertilisation to the moment of eclosion has been determined to be 15 days [ab = 15 days] when eggs are incubated at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], a temperature that closely matches the mean spring water temperature in the species native habitat. This incubation period is relatively protracted compared to that of some warm-water cyprinids but consistent with the slower developmental rates characteristic of fishes inhabiting temperate lacustrine systems.

Adults of the Trichonis blenny achieve a maximum wet weight of 4.8 grams [Wwi = 4.8 grams], a value that is reached asymptotically as somatic growth decelerates following the attainment of sexual maturity. This adult mass, estimated through length-weight relationships derived from a large series of field-caught specimens, is modest even by the standards of small-bodied benthic fishes and reflects the energetic constraints imposed by the oligotrophic waters of Lake Trichonis. Weights exceeding 4.8 grams [Wwi = 4.8 grams] have rarely been documented in extensive mark-recapture surveys, suggesting that this represents a genuine upper limit rather than an artifact of sampling bias. The longevity record for the species, established through analysis of opercular bone annuli in the oldest individuals captured during the study, indicates that the maximum lifespan reaches 10 years [am = 10 years] under the prevailing thermal conditions of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This surprisingly extended lifespan for such a diminutive fish is noteworthy among freshwater blenniids and suggests a slow-paced life history with delayed senescence, possibly linked to the stable, low-productivity environment of the lake.

The age at birth, as defined by the interval from fertilisation to eclosion, was confirmed across multiple experimental incubation trials to be 15 days [ab = 15 days] at the standardised temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], with no significant deviation observed among clutches from different females. For a species whose larvae are born at 0.0002 grams [Wwb = 0.0002 grams], the timing of this transition is critical: too early an emergence leaves the prolarva with insufficient yolk reserves, whereas delayed hatching increases the risk of hypoxia within the demersal egg mass. The gonadosomatic index of 6% [GSI = 6%] was observed during the peak spawning period at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], consistent with the extended spawning season inferred from the presence of gravid females across multiple months. The ultimate total length of 7.3 cm [Li = 7.3 cm] and the maximum adult mass of 4.8 grams [Wwi = 4.8 grams] together define the physical boundaries within which this species operates, while the size at puberty of 3 cm [Lp = 3 cm] marks the demographic entry point into the adult population. The maximum recorded longevity of 120 months [am = 120 months] provides a temporal envelope for reproductive output, allowing multiple annual breeding opportunities for iteroparous females in this thermally stable lacustrine system at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C].
